tiers.label: Open admission
tiers.detection: The college admits nearly everyone who applies, or it doesn't report an admission rate.
tiers.expects: A high school diploma. Placement scores decide whether you start in college-level math and English.
tiers.target: Finish your state's graduation requirements, reach the placement scores, and for career programs, finish a career and technical pathway and a credential. College-credit classes are options, not expectations.

tiers.label: Admits most applicants
tiers.detection: An admission rate of 50% or more.
tiers.expects: The state flagship's recommended classes, like Texas A&M's 4 English, 4 math, 4 science and 2 of one language, or UT Knoxville's 16 core courses.
tiers.target: A full college-prep core, with honors or college-level work in one or two of your major's rigor-first subjects by 11th or 12th grade. Strong grades matter more than the number of advanced classes.

tiers.label: Admits fewer than half
tiers.detection: An admission rate from 25% up to 50%.
tiers.expects: Rigor counts for more, and some majors are competitive. UT Austin encourages demanding classes beyond the level required.
tiers.target: Four years each of English, math and science, with college-level classes in your rigor-first subjects from 10th or 11th grade, keeping 12th grade as strong as 11th.

tiers.label: Very selective
tiers.expects: A balanced set of the most challenging classes available at your school, across the core subjects, including calculus for STEM. They don't expect every AP class.
tiers.target: As above, with calculus for STEM and economics, and three or more years of one language. Never take every AP class just because it's there.

guardrails.text: Plans are never scored or ranked by how many AP, IB or college-credit classes they have.
Suggest honors or college-level classes first in the few subjects that matter most for the student's goals.
No more than 3 college-level classes a year unless the student sets a different limit, and a gentle warning at 4 or more, with the reminder that teens need 8 to 10 hours of sleep.
Suggest doubling up or skipping ahead in math only after a B or better and only if the student opts in. A test score or placement exam can also show readiness.
Keep about five academic classes in 12th grade, but don't add new ones just for rigor.
Rigor is judged against what the student's school offers. A class the school doesn't offer never counts against the student.
Career and technical classes count as preparation, not a detour. In Texas, a program of study can meet an endorsement.
